section.title: The Remaining Tribes
section.sectionRationale: The distribution of the land is completed. By lot at Shiloh, Simeon, Zebulun, Issachar, Asher, Naphtali, and Dan each receive their inheritance, and at the very end, only after every tribe is settled, Joshua himself receives his portion, the town he requested. It is one movement, the finishing of the allotment, which shows God faithful to give each tribe its place and Joshua modeling the servant-leader who takes his own inheritance last.
section.thesis: God completes the inheritance for every tribe by lot at the sanctuary, keeping His promise down to the last portion, and the leader who had conquered the land takes nothing for himself until all the people are provided for, a picture of servant leadership that points to the greater Servant who secures His people's inheritance before His own glory.
section.frameNote: Seven beats: Simeon's inheritance within Judah, verses 1 to 9; Zebulun, verses 10 to 16; Issachar, verses 17 to 23; Asher, verses 24 to 31; Naphtali, verses 32 to 39; Dan, verses 40 to 48; and Joshua's own inheritance last of all, verses 49 to 51.

units.label: Simeon's inheritance within Judah
units.note: their inheritance lay within the territory of Judah

verses.text: The second {{goral|lot}} came out for the clans of the tribe of Simeon: Their inheritance lay within the territory of Judah
and included Beersheba (or Sheba), Moladah,
Hazar-shual, Balah, Ezem,
Eltolad, Bethul, Hormah,
Ziklag, Beth-marcaboth, Hazar-susah,
Beth-lebaoth, and Sharuhen, thirteen cities, along with their villages.
Ain, Rimmon, Ether, and Ashan, four cities, along with their villages,
and all the villages surrounding these cities as far as Baalath-beer (Ramah of the Negev). This was the inheritance of the clans of the tribe of Simeon.

The inheritance of the Simeonites was taken from the territory of Judah, because the share for Judah’s descendants was too large for them. So the Simeonites received an inheritance within Judah’s portion.

units.label: Zebulun's inheritance
units.note: the third lot came up for Zebulun

verses.text: The third lot came up for the clans of the tribe of Zebulun: The border of their inheritance stretched as far as Sarid.
It went up westward to Maralah, reached Dabbesheth, and met the brook east of Jokneam.
From Sarid it turned eastward along the border of Chisloth-tabor and went on to Daberath and up to Japhia.
From there it crossed eastward to Gath-hepher and to Eth-kazin; it extended to Rimmon and curved around toward Neah.
Then the border circled around the north side of Neah to Hannathon and ended at the Valley of Iphtah-el.
It also included Kattath, Nahalal, Shimron, Idalah, and Bethlehem. There were twelve cities, along with their villages.
This was the inheritance of the clans of the tribe of Zebulun, including these cities and their villages.

units.label: Issachar's inheritance
units.note: the fourth lot came out for Issachar

verses.text: The fourth lot came out for the clans of the tribe of Issachar:
Their territory included Jezreel, Chesulloth, Shunem,
Hapharaim, Shion, Anaharath,
Rabbith, Kishion, Ebez,
Remeth, En-gannim, En-haddah, and Beth-pazzez.
The border reached Tabor, Shahazumah, and Beth-shemesh, and ended at the Jordan. There were sixteen cities, along with their villages.
This was the inheritance of the clans of the tribe of Issachar, including these cities and their villages.

units.label: Asher's inheritance
units.note: the fifth lot came out for Asher

verses.text: The fifth lot came out for the clans of the tribe of Asher:
Their territory included Helkath, Hali, Beten, Achshaph,
Allammelech, Amad, and Mishal. On the west the border touched Carmel and Shihor-libnath,
then turned eastward toward Beth-dagon, touched Zebulun and the Valley of Iphtah-el, and went north to Beth-emek and Neiel, passing Cabul on the left.
It went on to Ebron, Rehob, Hammon, and Kanah, as far as Greater Sidon.
The border then turned back toward Ramah as far as the fortified city of Tyre, turned toward Hosah, and came out at the Sea in the region of Achzib,
Ummah, Aphek, and Rehob. There were twenty-two cities, along with their villages.
This was the inheritance of the clans of the tribe of Asher, including these cities and their villages.

units.label: Naphtali's inheritance
units.note: the sixth lot came out for Naphtali

verses.text: The sixth lot came out for the clans of the tribe of Naphtali:
Their border started at Heleph and the great tree of Zaanannim, passing Adami-nekeb and Jabneel as far as Lakkum and ending at the Jordan.
Then the border turned westward to Aznoth-tabor and ran from there to Hukkok, touching Zebulun on the south side, Asher on the west, and Judah at the Jordan on the east.
The fortified cities were Ziddim, Zer, Hammath, Rakkath, Chinnereth,
Adamah, Ramah, Hazor,
Kedesh, Edrei, En-hazor,
Iron, Migdal-el, Horem, Beth-anath, and Beth-shemesh. There were nineteen cities, along with their villages.
This was the inheritance of the clans of the tribe of Naphtali, including these cities and their villages.

units.label: Dan's inheritance and Joshua's portion last of all
units.note: they gave Joshua an inheritance among them

verses.text: The seventh lot came out for the clans of the tribe of Dan:
The territory of their inheritance included Zorah, Eshtaol, Ir-shemesh,
Shaalabbin, Aijalon, Ithlah,
Elon, Timnah, Ekron,
Eltekeh, Gibbethon, Baalath,
Jehud, Bene-berak, Gath-rimmon,
Me-jarkon, and Rakkon, including the territory across from Joppa.

(Later, when the territory of the Danites was lost to them, they went up and fought against Leshem, captured it, and put it to the sword. So they took {{yarash|possession}} of Leshem, settled there, and renamed it after their father Dan.)
This was the inheritance of the clans of the tribe of Dan, including these cities and their villages.
When they had finished distributing the land into its territories, the Israelites gave Joshua son of Nun an {{nachalah|inheritance}} among them,
as the LORD had commanded. They gave him the city of Timnath-serah in the hill country of Ephraim, as he requested. He rebuilt the city and settled in it.

These are the inheritances that Eleazar the priest, Joshua son of Nun, and the heads of the families distributed by lot to the tribes of Israel at Shiloh before the LORD at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting. So they finished dividing up the land.

goral.gloss: A lot, cast to determine God's decision. Each remaining tribe receives its portion by goral, so the whole distribution is seen as the LORD's own doing, not human negotiation. The repeated the lot came out for underlines that every tribe's place in the land was assigned by God, who orders the boundaries of His people's dwelling.

yarash.gloss: To take possession of, dispossess. When Dan lost its allotted coastal territory to enemy pressure, they went north and yarash, took possession of, Leshem, renaming it Dan. The note quietly signals both the difficulty Dan faced in its original portion and the ongoing struggle to possess the land, part of the incomplete conquest running through these chapters.

nachalah.gloss: Inheritance, allotted possession. After every tribe has received its nachalah, the people give Joshua his, the town he requested. That the conquering leader takes his inheritance last, only when all are provided for, models a servant leadership that seeks the people's good before its own, a pattern fulfilled in Christ.

basic.context: This chapter finishes the division of the land. One by one, the remaining tribes receive their inheritance by lot at Shiloh: Simeon (whose land lies inside Judah's large territory), Zebulun, Issachar, Asher, Naphtali, and Dan. There is a poignant note about Dan, whose coastal land was hard to hold, so they later migrated north and took a new city. Then comes the quiet climax: only after every tribe is settled do the people give Joshua his own inheritance, the modest town of Timnath-serah that he had requested. The great leader who had led the conquest waited until last and took a small portion. The chapter ends, so they finished dividing up the land. The question underneath is: what does it look like when God faithfully provides for all His people, and when a leader puts the people before himself?
basic.hermeneutics: This is historical narrative completing the allotment section, mostly land records with two telling notes: Simeon absorbed into Judah, and Joshua's inheritance taken last. The geography testifies to God's faithfulness in settling every tribe. Joshua's self-effacing example is presented positively and points to servant leadership. Dan's difficulty continues the honest thread of incomplete conquest.
basic.originalLanguages: Each tribe receives its portion by goral, by lot, as God's assignment. Dan, pressed out of its land, went and yarash, took possession of, a northern city. And Joshua receives his nachalah, his inheritance, last of all, after every tribe is provided for.
basic.typology: Joshua taking his inheritance last, after securing everyone else's, foreshadows Christ, the leader who seeks His people's good before His own glory, securing their inheritance through His self-giving. God's faithfulness in settling every tribe pictures the certainty of the inheritance He gives all His people.
basic.christ: Joshua, the conquering leader, waits to receive his own portion until all the people are settled, a faint shadow of the greater Joshua, Jesus, who did not grasp His glory but emptied Himself to secure His people's inheritance, and is exalted only after accomplishing their salvation. The completed allotment points to the inheritance Christ guarantees to all who are His.
basic.god: God is faithful to provide for every tribe, down to the last, ordering each portion by lot. He is the God who cares for the whole people, not just the prominent tribes, giving even absorbed Simeon and struggling Dan a place. And He honors the servant who puts others first, as the people give Joshua his inheritance at the end.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis 49 foretold Simeon being scattered in Israel, fulfilled in his absorption into Judah. Philippians 2 shows Christ emptying Himself and being exalted. Mark 10 says the greatest must be servant of all. And Joshua 21 concludes that not one of God's promises failed.
basic.oneStory: God completes the inheritance for every tribe, keeping His promise to the last portion, and Joshua the conquering leader takes his own share last of all. The faithful provision for the whole people and the servant leader who waits until the end point forward to Christ, who secures His people's inheritance before His own glory and settles them forever in the land of promise.

context.literary: This chapter completes a single numbered sequence that spans two chapters: Benjamin was already named the first lot in 18:11, and here the second through the seventh lots follow in order for Simeon, Zebulun, Issachar, Asher, Naphtali, and Dan, so chapters 18 and 19 together read as one continuous count from one to seven rather than as separate units. Six of those seven follow an almost identical shape, an ordinal marker, a border or city list, and a closing summary, this was the inheritance of the clans. Two details break that shape on purpose. Simeon's account never describes independent borders at all; it simply lists towns lying within Judah's territory and explains why, verses 1 and 9, an explanation none of the other six lots receives. And Dan's list ends with a parenthetical note, verse 47, that steps outside the land-deed style entirely to report something that happened later, after the main narrative's own timeframe, a rare authorial aside that looks past the events this chapter otherwise simply records. The chapter's real climax then breaks the pattern a second time: Joshua's own portion, verses 49 to 51, carries no ordinal number and no mention of a lot at all; the people simply give it to him, as the LORD had commanded, a deliberate departure from the sevenfold formula that has structured everything before it.
context.historical: Simeon's towns, Beersheba, Moladah, Ziklag, and the rest, sat in the dry southern Negev, a thin, marginal belt where population was sparse enough that the tribe's whole territory could be absorbed within Judah's much larger southern holding rather than needing its own separate boundary survey. Zebulun, Issachar, Asher, and Naphtali by contrast took the fertile valleys and hills around the Sea of Galilee and the plain of Jezreel, well-watered country that would support a denser population for centuries to come. Dan's original allotment lay on the coastal strip nearest Philistine territory, including Zorah and Eshtaol, towns that readers of Judges will recognize as the birthplace of Samson, whose own story of struggle against Philistine power grows directly out of the pressure this small tribe faced in exactly this district, Judges 13:2 and 13:24-25. That pressure explains the aside in verse 47: unable to hold its assigned coast, part of Dan went north instead and took Leshem by force, renaming it after their ancestor. The chapter closes at Timnath-serah, a town in the hill country of Ephraim that Joshua himself requested, a modest holding for the man who had led every campaign recorded in this book.
context.canonical: Simeon's absorption into Judah traces back further than this chapter admits on its own: Jacob's dying words had judged Simeon and Levi together for the violence they did at Shechem, vowing to divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel, Genesis 49:5-7, a sentence rooted in the massacre of Genesis 34:25-30. Simeon's story does not end here either; centuries later, in Hezekiah's day, Simeonite clans are still found migrating further south to find pasture, driving out the last remnant of Amalek at Mount Seir, 1 Chronicles 4:39-43, a tribe still finding its way even after the settlement recorded in this chapter. Dan's migration, told briefly and almost neutrally here, receives a much fuller and darker telling in Judges 18, where the same journey north is bound up with a stolen household idol and a shrine that becomes a byword for Israel's later apostasy once Jeroboam sets up a golden calf at that very city, 1 Kings 12:29-30. Joshua's own quiet portion at the end anticipates a theme the New Testament will draw out fully, that true honor in God's economy belongs to those who serve first and are served last.

hermeneutics.authorIntent: The writer includes two explanations that nothing else in this land-record genre requires. He tells us plainly why Simeon has no separate border, because Judah's share was too large for them, verse 9, and he adds an aside about Dan's later move north that steps outside the chapter's own timeframe to account for a gap between what was assigned and what was actually held. Neither explanation was strictly necessary to a bare record of towns and boundaries, which suggests the author cared that readers not be left guessing why two of the seven accounts look different from the rest. He then closes the whole allotment, all twelve tribes across five long chapters, on the single detail of Joshua's own house and lot, given last and given small. Moses, the first great mediator of this story, was shown the land from a mountain and died outside it without so much as a grave anyone could visit, Deuteronomy 34:4-6. Joshua, his successor, actually receives a portion, however modest, only once every other household in Israel has received its own. Placed side by side, the two accounts press a single lesson on the reader: God's servants do not measure their own worth by what they are given, and the truest leaders take their turn last rather than first.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription: The town lists and tribal boundaries are pure historical record, not commands, useful chiefly for tracing where Israel actually lived rather than for any transferable rule. More care is needed with Dan's brief note about taking Leshem, verse 47. Read on its own, in the plain, approving language this book normally uses for legitimate conquest, put it to the sword and took possession, it could easily be mistaken for a straightforward success story, Dan finally doing what earlier tribes in this book failed to do. Judges 18 tells the same event again at much greater length, and there the same migration is bound up with theft, a stolen idol, and the founding of an unauthorized shrine. Joshua's own brief account does not mention any of that, and readers should resist filling in either a full endorsement or a full condemnation from this chapter alone; the passage teaches us to hold a short, neutral report loosely until Scripture's own fuller account of the same event has had its say.

debates.question: What is the significance of Joshua receiving his inheritance last?

views.label: A model of servant leadership
views.case: The leader who led the conquest and oversaw the distribution does not seize the best land or take his portion first; he waits until every tribe is settled and then receives a modest town he requested, embodying the leader who seeks the people's good before his own, a pattern later crystallized in Jesus' teaching that the greatest must be servant of all, Mark 10:43-45.

views.label: A testimony to God's order and Joshua's contentment
views.case: That Joshua receives his inheritance as the LORD had commanded and asks only for one town shows both submission to God's order and personal contentment; he does not use his authority for self-enrichment but trusts God for his portion, closing the allotment on a note of humble faith rather than self-interest.

debates.bearing: Both readings commend Joshua: his placing himself last displays servant leadership and contentment, pointing to the greater Servant who secured His people's inheritance before entering His own glory.

debates.question: Does the brief note about Dan's migration and conquest of Leshem, verse 47, read as a faithful success or as an early warning sign?

views.label: A genuine, even encouraging, success
views.case: The verse uses the same approving vocabulary this book gives to legitimate victories elsewhere, went up, fought, captured, put to the sword, took possession, so on its own terms it looks like Dan finally doing forcefully what Ephraim and Manasseh had failed to do earlier in the book, driving out an enemy rather than settling for forced labor.

views.label: An early sign of the trouble Judges will fully expose
views.case: That Dan needed to migrate at all admits their assigned coastal towns could not be held, continuing this book's honest thread of incomplete possession, and the fuller account in Judges 18 shows the same journey accompanied by a stolen household idol and an unauthorized shrine that would trouble Israel for generations once a king later sets up a golden calf in that very city, 1 Kings 12:29-30.

debates.bearing: Joshua's narrator reports the bare fact without editorial comment either way, leaving Judges to supply the fuller and far darker picture; the two accounts of one migration need to be read together, since a note that looks like plain success here reads very differently once its sequel is told.

study.originalLanguages: Four features of the Hebrew carry this chapter's argument beyond the vocabulary already named. The word for tribe throughout, matteh, is the same word Hebrew uses for a staff or rod, the shepherd's or the leader's stick of authority; the very term for Israel's twelve constituent bodies pictures each one as a staff bundled together with the others, a small, physical image of tribal identity resting quite literally on a rod of authority long before any chapter, verse, or lot assigns it land. The refrain that structures nearly every section, for the clans of the tribe of, uses mishpachah, an extended family or clan grouping, the same word behind Israel's censuses in Numbers; every tribal boundary in this chapter is really a boundary drawn around a coalition of households rather than an abstract political unit. Dan's conquest of Leshem is described with a common but vivid idiom, they put it to the sword, in Hebrew literally by the mouth of the sword, lephi-cherev, an image that treats the blade's edge as a devouring mouth, the same idiom this book uses elsewhere for total, decisive victory, so its use here signals that whatever moral questions the episode later raises, the military action itself is described in the ordinary language of conquest rather than as some lesser or partial success. Finally, the town given to Joshua, Timnath-serah, appears in Judges under a slightly different spelling, Timnath-heres, the same consonants reordered, an odd but well attested variation between the two books. Heres in that second form sits close to the ordinary Hebrew word for the sun, which has led some readers to wonder about a solar association buried in the name; nothing in either text explains or confirms such a meaning, so it is worth noting as a curiosity rather than building any claim upon it. Staff bundled as tribe, household bundled as clan, a mouth that devours by the sword, and a town whose very name shifts under our hands: the chapter's Hebrew keeps returning to images of things gathered, wielded, and only partly fixed. Even the ordinal counting itself is worth a glance: Hebrew marks first through seventh with simple ordinal adjectives rather than any special vocabulary, yet the steady march from rishon, first, in chapter eighteen through shevi'i, seventh, here binds the two chapters into one arithmetic whole, so that a reader moving through the list is meant to feel each lot fall in its numbered turn until none are left, the plainest possible way of saying that no household was skipped and no share was left to chance.

typology.type: Simeon receiving no separate territory of its own but a portion carved out from within Judah's larger inheritance, 19:1 and 9
typology.fulfillment: One people is made to dwell inside another's allotted portion rather than possessing separately on its own footing, a small picture of how those once outside are grafted into a place and a root already established for someone else. It anticipates believers from the nations who do not grow their own independent root but are grafted in among the branches and now share the same rich root of the olive tree, receiving genuine inheritance yet always inside a portion God had first marked out for another, Romans 11:17-18.

typology.type: Dan's abandonment of its assigned coastal cities for an easier prize taken by its own initiative farther north, 19:47
typology.fulfillment: A tribe unwilling to keep contending for the hard cities of its own appointed portion goes elsewhere instead to seize a quicker, easier gain, and the fuller story in Judges shows that shortcut ending in a stolen idol and a shrine of false worship rather than faithful settlement. It stands as a caution against seeking by our own initiative, and on our own timetable, what God had already appointed us to receive by patient faith exactly where He first placed us.

typology.type: Joshua receiving his own inheritance last of all, in sharp contrast to Moses, who died outside the land altogether and received no earthly portion whatsoever, Deuteronomy 34:4-6
typology.fulfillment: Two great mediators of Israel's story are given, respectively, nothing at all and only the smallest, last share, and together they foreshadow the pattern completed in Christ, who owns all things by right yet during His earthly life had nowhere to lay His head, Matthew 8:20, receiving His full and universal inheritance only after finishing the work His people's salvation required, Hebrews 1:2-4.

study.christ: This chapter's pull toward Christ runs through two men who receive almost nothing where a reader might expect much. Moses led Israel out of Egypt, carried the law down from Sinai, and was shown the whole land from Pisgah's summit, and then died on the far side of the Jordan with no burial place anyone could ever visit, Deuteronomy 34:4-6. Joshua, who succeeds him and leads every campaign this book records, waits until the last household in Israel has its own ground before he receives so much as one town, and that only because he asked for it. Set beside each other, the two accounts trace an arc that culminates in a greater pattern still: one who owns the nations as His rightful inheritance by the Father's own decree, Psalm 2:8, chose instead to have nowhere to lay His head throughout His whole earthly ministry, Matthew 8:20, and was given His full inheritance, appointed heir of all things, only once He had completed the purifying work no one else could do, Hebrews 1:2-4. Dan's story supplies a second, darker thread. Zorah and Eshtaol, Dan's own towns listed here, verse 41, would soon produce Samson, a deliverer set apart from birth yet one whose strength repeatedly served his own appetite as much as his people's rescue, and whose victories, though real, never fully freed Israel from the Philistines he was raised up to resist. Every judge who follows this chapter, beginning in Dan's own territory, is a partial rescuer, strong enough to win a battle but never able to finish the war, and the book of Judges will say so explicitly by its own repeated, unhappy ending. Against that whole line of partial deliverers, Christ stands as the judge who does not merely win a battle within His people's history but ends the war outright, crushing every enemy under His feet until the last one, death itself, is put down for good, 1 Corinthians 15:24-26. What Moses could not enter, what Joshua entered only in the smallest share, and what every judge after Dan could only partly secure, Christ inherits, secures, and shares with His people in full.
study.god: God's care in this chapter shows itself most clearly in what He does not smooth over. Simeon carries a spoken judgment from Jacob himself for violence done generations earlier at Shechem, to be divided and scattered in Israel, and this chapter shows that judgment landing exactly as pronounced, Simeon absorbed into another tribe's territory rather than granted its own; yet even under that standing judgment, God still gives Simeon real towns, real villages, and a real place to live, discipline and provision running together rather than one canceling the other. Dan's difficulty is handled with the same restraint: God does not step in to hand Dan an easier alternative when the coastal Philistine cities prove too hard to take, and the tribe's own solution, migrating north under its own initiative, is recorded without either divine rebuke or divine blessing attached to it in this chapter, a striking silence that lets human choice stand on its own before Judges later reveals its cost. And when the whole distribution finally reaches its own leader, God's care shows in what is withheld rather than given: no lot is cast for Joshua, no elaborate ceremony marks the moment, only a brief note that the people gave him what he asked for, as the LORD had commanded, two verses closing out five chapters of far larger business. The chapter's very last line, so they finished dividing up the land, states outright what could easily have gone unremarked, that a promise reaching back through Moses to Abraham himself had now, after decades of wandering, war, and family upheaval, arrived at its own stated finish line. This is a God who lets consequences fall, who leaves room for human initiative even where it will later prove costly, and who is willing to let His own faithfulness be recorded in the plainest, least decorated sentence in the whole unit.

crossReferences.note: Simeon and Levi's violent revenge at Shechem lies behind Jacob's later judgment that the two brothers would be divided and scattered in Israel, the deeper background to why Simeon receives no separate territory in this chapter.
Moses is shown the whole land from Pisgah yet dies outside it with no inheritance and no known grave, the sharp contrast behind Joshua's own small but real portion at the close of this chapter.

Generations later, in Hezekiah's day, Simeonite clans are still migrating to find pasture, defeating the last remnant of Amalek at Mount Seir, showing Simeon's story of scattered, unsettled life continuing long after this chapter's record closes.

Zorah, listed here among Dan's original towns, is named again as Samson's birthplace, tying the tribal geography fixed in this chapter directly to one of Judges' most famous and most flawed deliverers.

The same migration north that Joshua reports in one brief, neutral verse is retold at far greater length in Judges, where it involves a stolen household idol and the founding of an unauthorized shrine, showing why a short account should never be mistaken for the whole story.

Centuries later Jeroboam sets up one of his golden calves at Dan, the very city this chapter's aside describes Dan capturing and renaming, so an act that reads as success in Joshua becomes the site of Israel's institutionalized idolatry.

Jesus says the Son of Man has nowhere to lay His head, a deeper echo of the pattern in Moses' unmarked grave and Joshua's small, late portion, the greater Son receiving even less outwardly than the last in line here.

Christ is appointed heir of all things only after making purification for sins, receiving His full inheritance after finishing His work, the pattern this chapter's leader, given his portion only once every household was settled, faintly foreshadows.

study.oneStory: Genesis had already marked one tribe for scattering because of old violence and had promised another a birthright doubled through adoption; by the time this chapter closes, both threads have played out exactly as spoken, Simeon folded into Judah's territory, Joseph's sons already settled with their double share two chapters earlier. What this chapter adds is the honest cost of settling twelve different households into one promised land: some, like Simeon, live inside a judgment as much as a gift, and others, like Dan, find their assigned ground harder to hold than expected and go looking for an easier one elsewhere, a shortcut that Judges will later show leading straight into an idol and a shrine that outlives the conquest generation by centuries. Against that mixed and costly record, the chapter closes on one deliberately small, deliberately late transaction: the man who led every battle receives, at the very end, the smallest and last portion, a sharp contrast to Moses before him, who led Israel to the border and received no portion at all. The line begun in Genesis, promise given, promise contested, promise partly forfeited through unbelief, runs forward from here through judges who win battles without ending wars, through a monarchy that will one day set up its own idols in Dan's very city, and finally to a King who receives His inheritance only after finishing, rather than merely starting, His people's rescue, appointed heir of all things once His work was done, and who welcomes into that inheritance even those who, like Simeon of old, never held an independent claim of their own but are given a share inside a portion first promised to another.

quiz.q: Where did the tribe of Simeon receive its inheritance?

options.text: Within the territory of Judah, because Judah's portion was too large.
options.note: Verses 1 and 9 explain Simeon's land was drawn from Judah's oversized share.

options.text: In the far north near Naphtali.
options.note: Simeon's land lay within Judah in the south, not in the far north.

options.text: East of the Jordan with Reuben and Gad.
options.note: The eastern land went to Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh; Simeon's lay within Judah.

options.text: Simeon received no inheritance at all.
options.note: Simeon did receive an inheritance, drawn from within Judah's territory.

quiz.q: What was notable about when Joshua received his inheritance?

options.text: He received it last of all, only after every tribe had been settled.
options.note: Verses 49 to 51 show Joshua taking his portion last, a model of servant leadership.

options.text: He took the first and best portion for himself.
options.note: The opposite: he waited until last and took a modest town he requested.
He did receive an inheritance, the town of Timnath-serah, but only after all others.

options.text: He seized several cities by force.
options.note: He received one town as the LORD commanded, taken last, not seized by force.

quiz.q: How was each tribe's portion determined?

options.text: By lot at Shiloh, so each portion was received as the LORD's own assignment.
options.note: The refrain the lot came out for marks each portion as God's assignment.

options.text: By the size of each tribe's army.
options.note: Portions were assigned by lot, not by military strength.

options.text: By Joshua's personal decision for each.
options.note: The lot, not Joshua's preference, determined each portion before the LORD.

options.text: By a vote among the tribal leaders.
options.note: It was decided by lot before the LORD, not by a vote.

quiz.q: How does Joshua taking his inheritance last point to Christ?

options.text: As the leader who secured the people's inheritance before his own, he foreshadows Christ who served and secured His people's good before His exaltation.
options.note: Joshua's servant leadership points to Christ in Philippians 2 and Mark 10:45.

options.text: It shows that leaders deserve the largest reward first.
options.note: The opposite: Joshua put himself last, modeling servanthood, not privilege.

options.text: It teaches that leaders should never receive anything.
options.note: Joshua did receive an inheritance; the point is that he put the people first, not that leaders get nothing.

options.text: It has no connection to Christ.
options.note: Joshua's placing himself last clearly foreshadows Christ, the Servant who secures His people's inheritance.

questions: God faithfully settled every tribe, even the small and struggling ones. How does it comfort you that God overlooks none of His people, however overlooked you may feel?
Joshua, the great leader, took his inheritance last, after everyone else was cared for. Where is God calling you to put others' good before your own?
Each portion was assigned by lot as God's own arrangement. How does trusting that your circumstances are ordered by a faithful God change the way you receive your lot in life?
Dan struggled to hold the land it was given. Where are you facing a struggle to lay hold of what God has promised, and how can you keep trusting Him in it?
The servant leadership of Joshua points to Christ, who secured your inheritance before His own glory. How does Christ's self-giving move you to serve others this week?

translationNotes.note: Simeon's inheritance within Judah reflects Jacob's word in Genesis 49:7 that Simeon would be divided and scattered in Israel.
This Bethlehem is a town in Zebulun's territory in the north, distinct from Bethlehem of Judah, the birthplace of David and of Christ.
Timnath-serah, Joshua's requested town, is also called Timnath-heres, as the BSB footnote notes; it was a modest portion for the nation's leader, taken last of all.
